title: LSAT Logical Reasoning: A Complete Guide to Arguments, Flaws, Assumptions, and Inference.
description: Logical Reasoning is two of the three scored sections on the current LSAT. This guide gives you one clear, repeatable method for every argument you meet. Since August 2024, Logic Games are gone and Logical Reasoning carries the larger share of your score. LSAT Logical Reasoning explains argument structure in plain English, so you can find the conclusion, see the gap and pick the answer under time pressure, without learning a new formal-logic vocabulary. Inside, you'll learn how to: Read the stimulus first: isolate premises, conclusions and unstated assumptions before you look at the answer choices. Group question types into families: strengthen, weaken, assumption and flaw questions become variations on one task, not unrelated puzzles. Spot engineered errors: correlation-causation gaps, circular reasoning and other common flaws. Pace with a two-pass approach: spend your 35 minutes on the questions that pay. Review like a high scorer: build your own decision path for naming each stem and keep an error log that turns practice into targeted review. Who it's for College students, career changers and future law school applicants who want a clear strategy they can apply to official material. The book is a strategy supplement: do your timed practice with official LSAT PrepTests (for example through LawHub), which are not included. title: LSAT Patterns and Traps: The Strategic Guide to Faster Reasoning and Smarter Answer Select
description: The LSAT reuses the same argument patterns and the same kinds of trap answers again and again. This guide teaches you to see them coming, so you choose faster and second-guess less. Since August 2024, Logic Games are gone: Logical Reasoning is two of the three scored sections and Reading Comprehension is the third. LSAT Patterns and Traps is a practical strategy guide for that test. It shows how arguments are built, how wrong answers are engineered, and how to stay accurate under the clock without turning prep into a memory drill. Inside, you'll learn how to: Read for structure first: premises, conclusion and the gap between them, before you look at the answer choices. Catch the three recurring flaws: hidden assumptions, correlation treated as causation, and shifts in scope. Take trap answers apart: recognise how tempting wrong choices are written and eliminate them on purpose, not on gut feel. Map Reading Comprehension passages: find the thesis, the counterargument and the evidence instead of memorising details. Turn practice into progress: keep a simple diagnostic error log and use pacing and stress habits that hold up on test day. Who it's for College students and future law school applicants who want a clear method they can apply to official material. The book is a strategy supplement: do your timed practice with official LSAT PrepTests (for example through LawHub), which are not included.
